title: What to Measure in the First Thirty Days
content:
###  **Worth Tracking** 

\*\*Conversations held\*\*, not just contacts attempted. This is the real unit of work in field outreach. 

\*\*Appointments scheduled\*\*, separated from general interest. A sales team works a calendar, not a list. 

\*\*Follow-up requests with timing\*\*, recorded with the date the homeowner named. In seasonal trades these often outnumber immediate appointments and represent real future revenue. 

\*\*Your own follow-up speed\*\* — what share of leads your team contacted, and how quickly. This frequently explains more variance than lead quality does. 

\*\*Cost per booked appointment\*\*, calculated the same way for every channel you run. 

\*\*What representatives heard.\*\* Patterns in objections, competitor pricing, and local perception are often the most immediately actionable output of a first month. 

###  **Two Measures That Mislead Early** 

\*\*Closed revenue in the first thirty days.\*\* Most home service sales cycles are longer than a month. Judging a channel on closes alone in week four measures the calendar, not the channel. 

\*\*Door count on its own.\*\* To be clear, activity should absolutely be tracked — we log doors approached, contacts made, conversations held, and notes left for every shift, and we share it weekly. The caution is against treating door count as the headline measure. A representative with fewer doors and more real conversations is outperforming, not underperforming, and a team measured on doors will learn to rush past the thing that actually produces results. 

###  **The Honest Standard** 

A first month should tell you whether the process is sound, whether the conversations are real, and whether the early pipeline is credible. It will not tell you the full return. That takes longer, and any channel promising otherwise is describing something other than how home service sales actually work.
